verdicts.flaw_description: Two of the four runs have outcome dates before the switch date: run One 'switched 4 May' but 'ran 6 minutes shorter by 29 March', and run Three 'switched 5 October' but shorter 'by 30 September' - the effect is recorded before the coolant was in use. The stated control also misses the units: 'Every shop ran its machines on the insert grade used the quarter before' yet 'every logged run was cut on a machine hired from outside', so the insert-grade control never covered the machines actually measured.

A named alternative cause reaches all four sections: 'The central syllabus doubled coursework's share of the final grade against the previous year, and every section was marked to that central syllabus.' Doubling coursework's weight is itself a reason completion would rise 6-11 points, and it applied to every unit measured, so the lab kit cannot be separated from it.

The numbers cover a narrower population than the claim: 'Figures cover the orders that cleared the staffed tills, and about a fifth of each store's orders went through self-checkout.' Roughly 20 percent of orders are excluded from the revenue-per-order figures, and self-checkout baskets differ systematically, so a 4-7 percent rise on staffed-till orders does not establish revenue per order rose overall.

The absence figures are restricted to survivors: they 'cover the pupils enrolled for the whole term, and about a fifth of each cohort left part-way through.' The ~20 percent of pupils who left - precisely the group most likely to have poor attendance - are dropped from the post-change figures, so the 4-7 percent fall in absence can be produced by the exclusion rather than by the timetable.
